title: Testing theory of mind in large language models and humans
extended_summary:
This paper investigates whether large language models (LLMs) show human-like performance on theory of mind tasks, meaning tasks that require tracking other agents’ beliefs, intentions, indirect meanings, irony, and faux pas. The central question is not about education or writing feedback, but about whether models such as GPT-4, GPT-3.5, and LLaMA2 produce responses comparable to humans across a broad battery of social-cognitive tests.

The authors repeatedly tested LLMs on established theory of mind measures including false belief, hinting, irony, faux pas, and strange stories, and compared model outputs with responses from large samples of human participants recruited online. They also created novel items and follow-up control experiments, especially around the faux pas task, to determine whether apparent successes or failures reflected real inferential capacity or artifacts such as response conservatism or bias. LLM sessions were treated as independent observations, and human responses were coded with predefined scoring criteria.

The population consisted of adult native English-speaking human participants recruited through Prolific, alongside multiple LLM systems tested in online chat environments. The work was conducted as an online experimental comparison rather than in schools or classrooms, and it does not involve students, teachers, instructional use, or formative feedback on writing. The paper therefore does not match the requested topic of comparative studies of LLM-generated formative feedback on student drafts.

The main conclusion is that GPT-4 often matched or exceeded human performance on several theory of mind tasks, while GPT models struggled on the faux pas task under its original wording. Follow-up analyses suggested this faux pas deficit reflected hyperconservative response behavior rather than a straightforward failure of inference. The authors argue that systematic, multi-test comparisons are necessary for meaningful human–LLM comparisons and that LLM outputs may resemble human mentalistic inference in some contexts while still differing importantly in underlying processes and decision behavior.
quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed empirical paper, but it is not an education intervention study and does not evaluate any grades 9-12 writing-feedback intervention. It studies LLM and human performance on theory-of-mind tasks, so it falls outside the K-12 comparative evidence framework requested for LLM formative feedback on student drafts.
impact_tier_rationale: No educational writing-feedback intervention or student draft-revision outcomes are studied, so there is no direct evidence of impact on high-school writing or feedback-related educational outcomes.
